title: Planet Earth & Climate · Episode 4
chapters: Ice cores: reading Earth's frozen diary

units.t: Planet Earth & Climate. Episode four.
In this episode: Ice cores: reading Earth's frozen diary, Climate change: the basics and Renewable energy.
Part one. Ice cores: reading Earth's frozen diary.
Drill deep into Antarctica and you pull up ancient air, volcanic fallout and the planet's temperature history, layer by layer, going back 800,000 years.
Snow that becomes a record.
In the coldest parts of Greenland and Antarctica, snow falls and never melts.
Each year's snow buries the last, compressing into granular firn and then solid ice.
The youngest ice sits on top and the oldest near the bedrock, sometimes more than three kilometres down.
Scientists drill out cores about ten centimetres wide and ship them frozen to laboratories.
Where snowfall is heavy, each year leaves a distinct layer, so layers can be counted like tree rings for tens of thousands of years.
Deeper down, the ice thins and flows, so ages come from flow models and volcanic markers.
Eruptions such as Tambora in 1815 leave sulphate spikes in both Greenland and Antarctic ice, tying the records to one calendar.
Bubbles of ancient air.
The most remarkable treasure in ice cores is air.
As firn turns to ice, the spaces between grains close off and trap tiny bubbles of atmosphere.
In the laboratory, scientists crush or melt samples under vacuum and measure gases such as carbon dioxide and methane.
There is one subtlety.
Air keeps circulating through the porous firn until it is sealed, typically several tens of metres down.
So the trapped air is younger than the ice around it, sometimes by thousands of years where snowfall is slow.
Scientists correct for the gap.
Australian researchers contributed greatly with cores from Law Dome, near Casey Station, where high snowfall gives a detailed record of carbon dioxide over the past two thousand years.
A thermometer in the water.
Ice itself records temperature.
Some water molecules contain heavier isotopes, such as oxygen-18 instead of oxygen-16, or deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen.
As moist air travels towards the poles and cools, the heavier molecules tend to fall out as rain or snow first.
So the colder the conditions, the fewer heavy molecules remain in the snow that finally lands on the ice sheet.
By measuring the ratio of heavy to light isotopes in each layer, scientists can reconstruct how temperature changed over time.
This isotope thermometer, developed largely by Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard from the 1950s, is a foundation of modern climate science.
800,000 years of climate.
The longest continuous ice core record comes from Dome C, high on the East Antarctic plateau, drilled by the European project EPICA.
It reaches back about 800,000 years and shows eight full cycles of ice ages and warmer interglacial periods.
Through all of them, carbon dioxide and temperature rise and fall together.
In cold glacial periods carbon dioxide sat around 180 parts per million.
In warm interglacials it rose to around 280 to 300.
Changes in Earth's orbit pace the cycles, with carbon dioxide acting as a powerful amplifier.
By the mid-2020s atmospheric carbon dioxide had passed 420 parts per million, far outside the range of the entire ice core record.
Abrupt change, older ice.
Greenland cores revealed something unsettling.
In the last ice age, temperatures there repeatedly jumped by several degrees, sometimes ten or more, within decades.
These Dansgaard–Oeschger events showed that climate can change abruptly.
The ice also records human history: lead from Roman mining and smelting settled in the snow, and dipped in times of war and plague.
Wildfires and dust storms leave traces too.
A puzzle remains.
About a million years ago, ice-age cycles lengthened from roughly 41,000 to about 100,000 years, and nobody is sure why.
In early 2025 the Beyond EPICA project reached bedrock at Little Dome C, recovering ice believed to be more than a million years old, though dating is still under way.
The key idea: Snow that never melts compresses into ice, forming a dated archive with the oldest layers at the bottom.
Part two. Climate change: the basics.
The physics has been understood since the 1800s.
Here's what's actually happening, what it means for Australia and what's being done.
The greenhouse effect.
Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which then gives off heat as infrared radiation.
Gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, CO₂, and methane absorb some of that infrared and send it back down, like a blanket.
This natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it, Earth's average temperature would be around minus 18 degrees instead of about 15 degrees.
The problem is thickening the blanket.
This isn't new science.
In 1856, Eunice Foote showed that a glass cylinder of CO₂ heated up more in sunlight than one of ordinary air.
John Tyndall measured how gases absorb heat in 1859, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that burning coal could warm the planet.
Where the CO₂ comes from.
Since the Industrial Revolution, humans have burned vast amounts of coal, oil and gas, and cleared forests.
Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million to over 420, higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years, based on air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice.
We know the extra carbon comes from fossil fuels because it carries a distinctive isotope signature.
Globally, the biggest sources are electricity and heat, industry such as steel and cement, transport, agriculture, land clearing and buildings.
Methane, from livestock, landfill and gas leaks, is a powerful short-lived gas.
In Australia, coal-reliant electricity has historically been the largest source, and emissions per person are among the highest in the developed world.
How much warmer.
The global average surface temperature has risen by roughly 1.
3 to 1.
4 degrees since the late 1800s, and the last decade was the warmest on record.
In 2024, the global average for a single year exceeded 1.
5 degrees above pre-industrial levels for the first time.
Australia's climate has warmed by about 1.
5 degrees since national records began in 1910, according to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO.
Land warms faster than oceans, which is why Australia's figure is higher than the global average.
Global sea level has also risen by more than 20 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is increasing.
What it means here.
For Australia, the effects include more frequent and intense heatwaves, and longer, more dangerous bushfire seasons in the south and east.
Some areas get heavier downpours, while the south-west and south-east get less cool-season rain.
The oceans around Australia have warmed and become more acidic, which stresses marine life.
During marine heatwaves, when seawater stays unusually hot for days or weeks, corals expel the algae that feed them and turn white.
The Great Barrier Reef has suffered several of these mass bleaching events since 2016.
Rising seas also add to the risk of flooding along low-lying coasts.
Paris and progress.
In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nearly every country agreed to keep warming well below 2 degrees and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.
5 degrees.
Scientists say that needs steep emissions cuts this decade and net zero, where remaining emissions are balanced by removals, around mid-century.
Every fraction of a degree matters: 2 degrees instead of 1.
5 degrees means more extreme heat, more species loss and far more damage to coral reefs.
Solutions are scaling quickly.
Solar power's cost fell by roughly 90 per cent in the 2010s.
Australia has more than four million rooftop solar systems, among the most per person in the world, and renewables now supply more than 40 per cent of the main grid's electricity.
Individuals help most through big choices: how they power and heat their homes, how they travel and how they vote.
The key idea: Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape to space, and the physics has been understood for over a century.
Part three. Renewable energy.
Australia has more rooftop solar per person than almost anywhere on Earth.
Here's how renewables work, and what makes the switch hard.
Why renewables.
Renewable energy comes from sources that are constantly replenished: sunlight, wind, flowing water and heat from the Earth.
Fossil fuels like coal and gas release carbon dioxide stored over millions of years when burned, and electricity generation has long been one of Australia's largest sources of greenhouse emissions.
Renewables produce almost no emissions while running, although making and installing them has a footprint.
Across their whole lifetime, solar, wind and hydro emit only a small fraction of the carbon of coal per unit of electricity.
They also use free fuel, a big reason the cost of renewable electricity has fallen so sharply over the past two decades.
Solar power.
Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity.
When light hits a cell of specially treated silicon, it knocks electrons loose and the cell's structure pushes them one way, creating direct current.
An inverter converts this to the alternating current used in homes.
A University of New South Wales team led by Martin Green developed the PERC cell design in the 1980s, which became the world's dominant solar cell technology for years.
Panel prices fell by around 90 per cent during the 2010s as mass production scaled up, largely in China.
Sunshine, rebates and falling prices helped more than a third of Australian houses install panels, around four million systems by the mid-2020s, among the highest rates per person in the world.
Wind and hydro.
Wind turbines capture the energy of moving air, spinning a generator.
Modern towers can exceed 100 metres, with blades longer than an Olympic swimming pool.
Wind speeds rise with height and power rises steeply with speed, so taller turbines produce much more.
The best resources are along the southern coast and in elevated areas, and South Australia gets well over half its electricity from wind and solar combined.
Wind suits solar because it often blows at night and in winter, when solar output is low.
Hydroelectric power, Australia's oldest large-scale renewable, uses water flowing downhill through turbines and can ramp up within minutes, a valuable backup when solar and wind dip.
Tasmania gets most of its electricity from hydro, and the Snowy Mountains Scheme is the mainland's biggest.
Storing energy.
At midday, rooftop solar can flood the grid, and wholesale prices sometimes go negative.
Then the sun sets and the wind drops.
Storage solves both problems.
In 2017, after a statewide blackout the year before, the Hornsdale Power Reserve was built near Jamestown in South Australia.
At 100 megawatts, it was then the world's largest lithium-ion battery, built in under 100 days.
It stabilises the grid, responding to faults in fractions of a second, faster than traditional power stations.
Home batteries store daytime solar for the evening.
Snowy 2.
0 is pumped hydro: it links two reservoirs, Tantangara and Talbingo, pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it when needed, storing energy for days rather than hours.
Its estimated cost has blown out from about $2 billion to more than $20 billion.
Trade-offs and targets.
Solar and wind are variable, so the grid needs storage, backup such as gas, and smarter demand management.
Good sites are often far from cities, so thousands of kilometres of new transmission lines are needed, which can face strong opposition.
Wind and solar farms use large areas of land, and turbines can affect birds and landscapes.
Panels, turbines and batteries need mined minerals, and recycling at scale is still developing.

Still, renewables supplied roughly 40 per cent of electricity in the main eastern and southern grid by the mid-2020s, up from under 10 per cent in the early 2000s, and in 2022 the federal government set a target of 82 per cent by 2030, though progress is debated.
For a home system, get several quotes from accredited installers and check rebates.
The key idea: Renewable energy comes from naturally replenished sources and produces almost no emissions while running.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How do scientists date ice too deep for its yearly layers to be counted?
Answer. By using ice-flow models and volcanic markers.
Question two. Why is the natural greenhouse effect important?
Answer. Without it, Earth would be far too cold.
Question three. Why has the cost of renewable electricity fallen so sharply?
Answer. Free fuel and mass-produced equipment have cut costs.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
